strengths: Significance: Proactively discovering reusable intermediate lemmas addresses a practical bottleneck in formal mathematics. The reported three Mathlib merges (Section 6.2) provide encouraging, albeit small-scale, evidence of usefulness.

Evaluation: The benchmark spans 109 seed files and multiple mathematical domains. Evaluating seven model configurations, reporting repair-round performance, and auditing 138 model-unsolved statements provide useful empirical coverage. The 107 human-proved instances are particularly valuable evidence that some remaining tasks are solvable.

Presentation and reproducibility: The pipeline is understandable, and the appendices provide prompts, extraction rules, inference settings, and a Lean version. The discussion openly acknowledges semantic duplication, repair-induced semantic drift, and upstreaming effort. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—proof verification is insufficient as specified. Appendix B.4 accepts a proof whenever Lean produces no error-level diagnostics. Lean can accept declarations containing sorry with a warning, so this criterion does not establish a completed proof. Moreover, the prover outputs the entire declaration, but no check is described that its type matches the original target or that it introduces no unauthorized axioms. This does not demonstrate that the reported proofs are invalid, but it leaves the central claims of 1,812 verified proofs and the success rates unsupported by the documented verifier. The authors need explicit target-preservation and axiom/dependency checks, followed by revalidation.

Significance—novelty and usefulness of the generated library are not established at scale. Section 4.2 treats failure of default aesop as evidence of semantic novelty. However, an existing theorem can fail this test because aesop does not automatically retrieve and apply every Mathlib result. Consequently, low aesop success does not establish that the candidates fill missing library gaps. The three reported merges are promising, but there is no representative novelty audit, quantified human editing effort, or downstream demonstration that the larger library improves formalization.

Originality and methodological evidence: The four stages combine familiar conjecture generation, LLM judging, compiler-guided repair, and proof generation. The potentially distinctive contribution is the folklore-mining objective and resulting artifacts, rather than an established new algorithm. There is no comparison with the cited LeanConjecturer-style approach, simpler end-to-end generation, or ablations of the Judge and Formalizer. Thus, claims that this decomposition is essential and more effective remain untested; generation cost and useful-lemma yield would be important comparison metrics.

Soundness—benchmark validity and audit conclusions are overstated. Experts prove 107/138 sampled residuals, but Appendix D identifies missing hypotheses in 21 of the 31 remaining cases, making those statements false as written. These are substantive benchmark errors even when the underlying intuition is reasonable. The approximately 88% solvability estimate is not a demonstrated theoretical ceiling: human failure does not establish impossibility, and sampling two lemmas per seed requires attention to weighting and uncertainty. Additionally, open-book, AI-assisted experts outperforming closed-book models does not isolate a deficit in deep structural reasoning. Reporting the audit is a strength; the stronger conclusions drawn from it are not justified.

Soundness—several experimental interpretations exceed the evidence. The union of seven configurations receives substantially more inference effort than any individual model, so its 44.99% success versus 22.32% does not establish that diversity is more valuable than scale without a compute-matched baseline. Differences between independently trained models likewise do not isolate the effects of distillation, training regime, or architecture. These results support descriptive performance comparisons, not the broader causal conclusions in Section 5.2.

Reproducibility and presentation: The supplied manuscript provides no usable artifact link or concrete generated proof listings, and it does not specify a pinned Mathlib revision. Anonymous artifacts could support inspection without identifying the authors. The repair budget is also inconsistent: Algorithm 1 uses K attempts, while Appendix C defines Success@2 as an initial attempt plus two repairs. Finally, Table 1 labels Judge-approved candidates 'Correct' despite the judge being fallible. These issues need resolution to make the benchmark reliably reproducible and its reported guarantees clear.

strengths: Significance: Targeting missing reusable lemmas addresses a credible bottleneck in everyday formalization. Coverage across 109 Mathlib files and three broad domains makes this a potentially useful complement to competition-mathematics benchmarks.

Methodology: Separating discovery, semantic judgment, statement repair, and proof generation is a sensible engineering design. The reported evaluation spans seven model configurations and includes domain-level results and repair-turn breakdowns.

Evidence: The audit constructs proofs for 107 of 138 sampled model-unsolved statements, providing meaningful evidence that many generated challenges are solvable. The three reported Mathlib merges offer preliminary evidence of practical utility, although supporting artifacts are omitted.

Presentation and limitations: The pipeline is clearly organized, with pseudocode, prompts, and substantial configuration details. The conclusion appropriately acknowledges imperfect deduplication, semantic drift, and upstreaming effort. I identify no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—proof acceptance is insufficiently specified. Appendix B.4 explicitly accepts generated code whenever Lean returns no error-level diagnostics. Lean can compile declarations containing sorry with warnings, and newly introduced axioms can also pass compilation. Furthermore, the prover outputs the entire declaration, but no check is described that its statement matches the original target. Thus, the documented rule does not establish the central claim of 1,812 verified proofs of the benchmark statements. This does not demonstrate that the artifacts are invalid, but explicit checks for forbidden dependencies and target preservation, followed by revalidation, are essential.

Soundness—semantic novelty is not established. Section 4.2 treats failure of default aesop as evidence that a statement fills a nontrivial library gap. Existing theorems and straightforward reformulations can evade this tactic. There is no systematic library search, semantic duplicate audit, or quantified expert assessment of usefulness. The acknowledged limitation is consequential because discovering missing folklore, rather than generating plausible statements, is the primary contribution.

Soundness—benchmark validity and audit conclusions are overstated. Appendix D identifies missing hypotheses in 21 of 31 audit failures; such omissions make the stated propositions false, regardless of whether the underlying intuition is reasonable. The comparison between open-book, AI-assisted humans and closed-book models on a subset selected specifically for model failure cannot isolate a deficit in deep structural reasoning. Moreover, extrapolating 107/138 successes to approximately 88% overall solvability requires accounting for the stratified sampling and uncertainty; it is not a demonstrated theoretical upper bound.

Originality and methodology: The architecture combines familiar prompting, LLM judgment, and compiler-feedback repair. The potentially distinctive contribution is the folklore-mining objective, but no comparison with LeanConjecturer, a simpler generation-and-proving pipeline, or an ablation establishes an advantage. Rejecting many candidates does not establish the Judge's value: 46% of its audited rejections were valid, and its effect on final valid-lemma yield per unit compute is unmeasured.

Significance—practical impact remains weakly quantified. Three reported merges support a promising pilot, but do not establish that the broader collection contains thousands of useful missing facts. The manuscript supplies no concrete generated statement/proof examples, downstream proof-completion study, representative usefulness audit, or accounting of human edits and selection effort. The claim that the collection effectively closes library gaps therefore exceeds the evidence.

Experimental interpretation: Several conclusions in Section 5 are stronger than the comparisons support. A seven-configuration union receives substantially more inference effort than one model, so its higher coverage does not establish that diversity is more valuable than scale without a matched-budget baseline. Likewise, comparisons between differently trained models cannot isolate distillation, architecture independence, or library fine-tuning as causal explanations. The descriptive performance results remain useful, but these interpretations require controlled evidence.

Reproducibility and presentation: Although prompts and several runtime settings are provided, the supplied manuscript has a blank code/data availability address and omits upstream PR details. Consequently, the benchmark, proof-validation safeguards, and merge claims cannot be independently inspected from the submission. An exact Mathlib revision, accessible anonymized artifacts, audit proofs and counterexamples, and a consistent repair-budget specification are needed: Algorithm 1 describes K attempts, whereas the experiments use an initial attempt plus two repairs. These gaps materially limit reliable reuse.

strengths: Significance: Proactively generating reusable library lemmas addresses a practical bottleneck in formal mathematics. The reported three Mathlib merges provide encouraging, albeit small-scale, evidence of utility beyond benchmark performance.

Empirical breadth: The study covers 109 seed files, 4,028 statements, and seven model configurations across foundational, applied, and abstract mathematics. The domain breakdowns and repair-turn results provide useful descriptive comparisons.

Quality assessment: Auditing 138 model-unsolved statements and 53 judge-rejected candidates is valuable. Experts reportedly proved 107 residual statements, establishing that many unsuccessful model attempts concern solvable problems.

Presentation and transparency: The modular pipeline is understandable, and the appendices provide prompts, extraction rules, and substantial configuration detail. The acknowledged limitations concerning semantic duplicates, semantic drift, and upstreaming effort are appropriate. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—proof verification is insufficiently specified: Appendices A.2 and B.4 explicitly accept generated code whenever Lean reports no error-level diagnostics. Lean can accept declarations containing sorry with warnings; error-free compilation alone does not establish a complete proof. Moreover, the prover regenerates the entire declaration, without a documented check that its proposition matches the original target. Excluding sorry-dependent proofs and unauthorized axioms, and checking target preservation, are essential to substantiate the reported 1,812 verified proofs and success rates. This identifies an inadequate documented acceptance rule, not evidence that particular outputs are invalid.

Soundness—novelty is not established: Section 4.2 uses failure of default aesop as evidence of semantic novelty. Existing Mathlib facts may require explicit invocation or rewriting and remain inaccessible to this tactic. Consequently, the experiment does not establish that most generated statements fill missing library gaps. A systematic library comparison and expert assessment of novelty and usefulness are needed.

Benchmark validity: Appendix D identifies missing hypotheses in 21 of 31 unsuccessful audit cases. Such omissions make the stated propositions false, even when their underlying intuition is reasonable. Describing these as distinct from mathematical errors understates benchmark noise. The approximately 88% solvability estimate is an extrapolation from a stratified sample, without uncertainty or explicit population weighting, rather than an established theoretical ceiling.

Unsupported interpretations: Open-book, AI-assisted human success cannot isolate a deficit in models' deep structural reasoning under closed-book evaluation. Similarly, the seven-model union receives substantially more attempts than an individual model, so its advantage does not establish that diversity is preferable to scale without a compute-matched comparison. Cross-model differences also do not isolate the effects of distillation, architecture, or training methodology.

Originality and methodological evidence: The distinction from LeanConjecturer and other library-expansion systems is primarily the intended folklore focus. There is no comparative evaluation establishing better novelty, usefulness, or yield, and no ablation supporting the claimed necessity of the four-stage architecture. The rejected-candidate audit measures correctness among rejections; it does not itself establish high precision among accepted candidates.

Practical significance and reproducibility remain uncertain: Three selected merges do not establish broad usefulness of the generated collection, and downstream formalization benefits and human editing effort are unmeasured. Repository links and example code are omitted from the supplied manuscript, preventing inspection of the central artifacts. An exact Mathlib revision, audit artifacts, and complete verification safeguards are particularly important. Despite the promising objective, these unresolved issues affect the central correctness and library-expansion claims and prevent acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Mining reusable intermediate lemmas addresses a practical bottleneck in formal mathematics. The 4,028-statement benchmark and reported 1,506 checked proofs could become useful resources beyond competition-style theorem proving.

Methodology and presentation: The four-stage pipeline is clearly described, with prompts, extraction rules, repair budgets, construction statistics, and domain-level results. Separating statement repair from proof generation makes failures easier to diagnose.

Evaluation: The human audits provide meaningful evidence that many model-unsolved statements are provable: experts proved 107/138 main-audit instances and 79/94 additional residual instances. Reporting both sequential repair results and explicitly distinguished independent-sampling results is helpful.

Practical relevance: The three reported Mathlib merges illustrate plausible API contributions. The paper appropriately presents this as a small, curated pilot rather than evidence that all generated lemmas meet upstream standards.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript candidly acknowledges generation-model dependence, imperfect novelty filtering, statement drift during repair, and maintenance requirements. Its selective upstreaming policy appropriately considers volunteer maintainers’ review burden.
weaknesses: Soundness—verification does not establish preservation of the target theorem as described. Sections 3.2.4 and B.4 ask the model to regenerate the entire declaration, then accept a compiling file that passes a token-based bypass screen. No explicit check ensures that the returned theorem has exactly the original proposition under the original assumptions, or even that the required declaration is present. A changed conclusion or added hypothesis can compile without any prohibited keyword. This is an unresolved gap in the evidence supporting both the success rates and the verified-library claim; the evaluator should insert proofs into immutable declarations or independently check target types and dependencies.

Significance—actual library-gap coverage is insufficiently established. Failure of default aesop does not demonstrate semantic novelty, nonredundancy, or usefulness. There is no representative audit of these properties across the 1,506 proofs and no downstream experiment measuring improved proof success or reduced formalization effort. Three selected merges demonstrate possibility, but cannot establish the broader claim of supplying over a thousand missing folklore facts; one of the six pilot candidates was explicitly rejected as redundant.

Benchmark validity remains problematic. Appendix D identifies missing necessary hypotheses in 25/138 audited residuals and false statements in another 5/138. Missing necessary hypotheses also make statements invalid as posed; distinguishing them from 'fundamental mathematical errors' does not resolve their effect on evaluation. Keeping such targets without validity labels confounds prover difficulty with impossibility. A verified evaluation subset or a clearly separated conjecture-discovery protocol would make scores substantially more interpretable.

Originality and pipeline efficacy are not adequately demonstrated relative to existing conjecturing systems. The distinction from LeanConjecturer and Lemmanaid rests largely on an intended focus on folklore, while the implementation uses seed-file prompting and familiar judge/repair/prove stages. There is no direct comparison or controlled evaluation showing greater novelty, usefulness, or yield. Appendix F tests a hypothesis-listing prompt, but does not establish the benefit of the four-stage factorization. In particular, the rejected-candidate audit finds 46% valid statements, making a matched-budget assessment of the Judge important.

Several interpretations exceed the experimental evidence. The seven-model union uses substantially more inference than any individual model, so its higher coverage does not establish that diversity is more valuable than scale without a compute-matched baseline. Likewise, cross-model differences do not isolate effects of training strategy, distillation, or parameter count. Claims about memorization, hallucination, and abstract reasoning are not supported by a quantified error analysis.

Reproducibility is only partial despite useful appendices. Configuration descriptions include defaults and examples rather than a complete per-model specification, and environment adjustments are introduced 'when required by specific models.' The audits omit sufficient detail about seed selection, annotator procedures, effort budgets, and adjudication to assess selection effects. The unusually low 0.32% Pass@16 result for the 8B specialist also warrants a known-benchmark sanity check and a failure breakdown before being treated as evidence of benchmark difficulty.

strengths: Significance: Expanding reusable formal libraries is a useful problem beyond competition theorem proving. The reported 1,506 checked proof artifacts and 4,028 benchmark statements span substantial mathematical breadth. Three manually curated Mathlib merges provide concrete, though limited, evidence of practical value.

Soundness: The paper distinguishes type checking from provability, reports model-unsolved statement audits, and supplements the 107/138 main audit with a held-out 79/94 result. These audits substantiate that many unsolved instances are valid mathematical targets.

Presentation and reproducibility: The modular pipeline is clearly described, with prompt templates, extraction rules, repair budgets, inference settings, and a Lean toolchain version. Domain-level results and sequential repair breakdowns make the evaluation reasonably interpretable.

Limitations and ethics: The authors acknowledge generation-model dependence, semantic redundancy, repair-induced changes, and curation costs. The selective upstreaming policy appropriately respects volunteer maintainers and avoids advocating bulk submission.
weaknesses: Soundness—target preservation is not established. Section 3.2.4 and Appendix B.4 accept a generated full Lean declaration based on successful compilation and a lexical proof-bypass screen. They do not describe checking that its elaborated proposition matches the original benchmark target under unchanged assumptions. A modified conclusion or additional hypothesis could pass these checks without solving the requested problem. Algorithm 1 comments that it verifies a proof of S, but its explicit check receives only the generated code. This is an unresolved verification gap, not evidence that particular reported proofs are incorrect.

Significance—large-scale discovery of missing, useful lemmas remains unvalidated. Declaration-name checks and failure of default aesop do not establish semantic novelty relative to Mathlib. There is no representative novelty/usefulness audit or downstream experiment measuring gains from the generated library. The six selectively submitted candidates, including one rejected as redundant, cannot establish that the larger collection consists of missing folklore facts. The honest acknowledgment of this limitation is welcome, but it limits the central contribution.

Benchmark validity is materially compromised by false targets. Appendix D identifies missing hypotheses in 25 of 138 audited residuals and another five statements as false as stated. Missing necessary hypotheses also make a formal proposition invalid; distinguishing these from 'fundamental mathematical errors' does not remove the evaluation problem. Keeping such targets in the denominator confounds proof difficulty with impossibility, particularly across domains. The seed-stratified audit supports the existence of many valid residuals, but does not precisely calibrate benchmark-wide validity. A validated evaluation subset or a separate conjecture-assessment task is needed.

Originality and methodological support are limited. The implementation combines prompted conjecturing, LLM judging, compiler-guided repair, and proof search. Relative to the discussed LeanConjecturer and Lemmanaid work, the principal distinction is the folklore-mining objective, whose novelty and usefulness criteria are not operationally verified. No direct synthesis baseline or judge/formalizer ablation establishes the claimed necessity of the four-stage design. Finding that 46% of sampled judge rejections were valid particularly motivates a compute-matched evaluation of that filter.

Several experimental interpretations exceed the evidence. Section 5.2 attributes differences to training strategy and recommends diversity over scale, but the models differ in numerous uncontrolled ways. Comparing a seven-model union against one model also increases inference expenditure substantially; no matched-budget repeated-sampling baseline isolates diversity. Closed-book scores are useful measurements, but cannot establish the claimed causes of abstract-domain failures or practical performance with library retrieval.

Reproducibility needs stronger evaluation diagnostics. Appendix A provides useful general settings, but insufficient model-specific serving, truncation, and failure accounting to explain striking results such as Goedel-8B solving only 13/4,028 problems at Pass@16. The human audits also lack clear expert counts, effort budgets, and reproducible instance-selection details. These omissions matter because the validity estimates and unusually low baseline results underpin the benchmark's interpretation.

strengths: Significance: Mining reusable intermediate lemmas addresses a practical bottleneck in formal mathematics. The reported 4,028 statements and 1,506 Lean-checked proof artifacts span substantially broader mathematics than competition-focused benchmarks.

Practical evidence: Three curated lemmas reportedly merged into Mathlib provide concrete evidence that selected outputs can be useful. Appendix E explains their mathematical roles and supplies readable proofs. The paper appropriately distinguishes this small pilot from evidence of library-wide adoption.

Soundness: The manual audits are valuable. Experts prove 107/138 sampled model-unsolved statements, and a separate held-out audit proves 79/94. These results substantiate that many residual instances are valid challenges rather than merely false conjectures.

Presentation and reproducibility: The modular workflow is clearly explained, with prompt templates, pseudocode, repair budgets, Lean version, domain-level results, and approximate API costs. Separating statement elaboration from proving makes intermediate failure modes observable.

Limitations and ethics: The paper candidly acknowledges semantic duplication, statement drift during repair, generation-model dependence, and library maintenance costs. Selective upstreaming and explicit consideration of volunteer reviewer burden are responsible choices.
weaknesses: Soundness—verification of the original target is insufficiently specified. Appendix B.4 asks models to regenerate the entire declaration, while Algorithm 1 checks the resulting file and applies a lexical proof-bypass screen. No explicit check establishes that the generated theorem has exactly the original proposition under the original context. A changed conclusion or added hypothesis can compile without any forbidden token. This does not demonstrate that reported proofs are incorrect, but leaves a material gap in the central verification claim. The evaluation should check generated proof terms against immutable target types and audit their dependencies.

Significance—missingness and usefulness are not established at scale. Failing default aesop does not establish semantic novelty: an existing theorem may require an explicit invocation, rewriting, or specialization. Discovery sees individual seed files rather than searching the repository, and one of six selected upstream candidates was rejected as redundant. A representative redundancy/usefulness audit and a downstream experiment measuring proof success or effort with the generated library are needed to support claims of filling thousands of library gaps.

Benchmark validity remains a substantial concern. Appendix D identifies 25 missing-hypothesis cases and five false statements among 138 audited residuals. Statements lacking necessary hypotheses are invalid as stated, even when their underlying intuition is reasonable. Consequently, the headline success rates mix proving difficulty with invalid targets. The audits support the existence of many valid residuals, but do not establish a clean benchmark or precise validity-adjusted scores; a verified evaluation subset or explicit separation of conjecture assessment and theorem proving would improve reliability.

Originality and methodological evidence are limited. The four stages combine familiar generation, LLM judging, compiler repair, and proof search. The distinction from LeanConjecturer and related library-expansion work is primarily the intended folklore focus, without a controlled comparison demonstrating better novelty, utility, or cost. There is also no matched-budget ablation establishing the Judge's benefit, despite 46% of its audited rejected candidates being valid.

Experimental conclusions exceed the controls. The seven-model union receives substantially more aggregate inference than any individual model, so its improvement does not establish that diversity is more valuable than scale. Likewise, comparisons across differently trained models do not isolate the effects of library fine-tuning, competition training, or distillation. The exceptionally low Goedel-8B Pass@16 result warrants implementation and prompting sanity checks before being used as supporting evidence of difficulty.

Reproducibility is only partial despite useful implementation detail. The manuscript does not fully specify seed-selection procedures, per-model inference configurations, or expert-audit selection and adjudication procedures. These details matter for reproducing the distribution, assessing model comparisons, and interpreting the seed-stratified validity estimates.
